paper_metadata.title: Qudit-based scalable quantum algorithm for solving the integer programming problem

summary: The paper presents a gate-based qudit algorithm for integer programming with 5 variables, 4 constraints, and d=3, demonstrated numerically on a non-linear instance whose feasible region has 6 states out of 243. The reported optimal solution is |01002⟩ with objective value 4, and the authors compare against branch-and-bound (358 nodes), brute force (243 computations), and Google OR-Tools CP-SAT, while claiming asymptotic scaling O(m·n^2·log d + d^(n/2) + n/ε_QPE).

experiments.description: Gate-based qudit quantum algorithm for solving a general integer programming problem, including constraint satisfaction via distillation and Grover amplitude amplification, followed by cost-function optimization via QPE and controlled rotation. Demonstrated numerically on a 5-variable, 4-constraint non-linear integer program with d=3.

algorithm.variant: Qudit-based scalable quantum algorithm with constraint distillation, Grover amplitude amplification, QPE-based cost encoding, and controlled rotation
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Uniform superposition over qudit register; QPE register initialized in |0...0>; ancilla initialized in |0> and |-> as required by subroutines

problem_formulation.encoding_details: n d-dimensional qudits encode n integer variables xi∈{0,...,d-1}; m qubits encode constraint satisfiability; feasible states are post-selected by measuring all constraint qubits in |1>
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Constraint distillation function fi(Ci,hi)=2 floor(Ci/hi) maps feasible states to qubit |1> and infeasible states to |0>; Grover amplitude amplification used to boost probability of all-ones constraint register; post-selection on constraint register

problem_instance.description: Non-linear non-convex integer program used as numerical demonstration
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical circuit simulation; compared against branch-and-bound, brute force, and Google OR-Tools CP-SAT; reported optimal solution probability and repetition count for target success probability 0.99

implementation_details.classical_solver: branch and bound; brute force; Google OR-Tools CP-SAT (baselines only)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical computation of cost upper bound Cub and relaxed-problem bound Ccont; branch-and-bound lower bound used to estimate repetitions
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure qudit register to decode optimal integer assignment; verify constraint satisfaction classically

speedup_claims.factor: exponential reduction; dn/2 improvement over brute force
speedup_claims.conditions: worst-case feasible region size 1; general polynomial integer programming problem; gate-based qudit algorithm
speedup_claims.caveats: Claim is asymptotic and worst-case; actual runtime depends on feasible-region size and QPE precision.

speedup_claims.factor: faster than best-known exact classical algorithm O((log n)^3 n) for the stated general IP setting
speedup_claims.conditions: as stated in the paper for general IP; especially non-linear problems
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper presents this as a complexity comparison, not an empirical benchmark.

speedup_claims.factor: Grover-style quadratic speedup in search over feasible states: O(d^(n/2)) iterations
speedup_claims.baseline_method: unstructured classical search over d^n states
speedup_claims.conditions: when the feasible region contains a single state
speedup_claims.caveats: This is embedded inside the full algorithm and depends on successful constraint distillation.

speedup_claims.factor: ≤19 repetitions to reach target success probability 0.99
speedup_claims.caveats: This is repetition count for success amplification, not a wall-clock speedup.

speedup_claims.factor: quantum algorithm better than classical exact and approximate methods for sufficiently large n in the plotted comparison
speedup_claims.baseline_method: Lenstra, Kannan, Frank-Tardos, Reis-Rothvoss, LP+rounding, and heuristics
speedup_claims.conditions: for the parameter choices shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4
speedup_claims.caveats: The comparison is based on asymptotic scaling curves, not direct runtime measurements.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(d^n) brute force; best-known exact classical algorithm O((log n)^3 n) as stated in paper for general IP; many classical methods restricted to linear IP
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: Worst-case amplitude amplification requires ~d^(n/2) Grover iterations; total leading-order time O(m·n^2·log d + d^(n/2) + n/ϵ_QPE)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established experimentally; the paper gives asymptotic scaling and a numerical example only.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Gate-based qudit circuit with 5 qudits for variables, 4 qubits for constraints, and an ancilla qubit for the controlled rotation; QPE register size l=4 in the demonstration.
limiting_factors: No real QPU or hardware benchmark
QPE precision and Grover repetition overhead
Large gate complexity from qudit-controlled constraint unitaries
Classical baselines are only compared on a toy 5-variable instance

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports a numerical implementation in Python and does not name a real QPU or simulator backend.

num_qubits inferred from the demonstration setup: 5 qudits for variables plus 4 qubits for constraints plus 1 ancilla qubit = 10 total qubits/qudit-register units counted as quantum registers; the paper explicitly states 5 qudits and 4 qubits, and later introduces 1 ancilla qubit for the rotation step.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported; only asymptotic gate/time complexity and repetition counts are given.
The paper is gate-based and explicitly excludes annealing; no annealer runs are present.
The paper claims an asymptotic reduction from O(d^n) to O(m·n^2·log d + d^(n/2) + n/ε_QPE), but provides only a numerical simulation and no experimental quantum-vs-classical hardware benchmark.
